\chapter{Green and Yellow}
\label{ch:ar-green-and-yellow}
\hlchaptermodality{22}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name green and yellow in Arabic and trace aṣfar to the same root as ṣifr, 'zero'.}

Say akhḍar beside khuḍār, 'vegetables', then aṣfar beside ṣifr, and follow ṣifr into English zero and cipher.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ar{أخضر}, \ar{أصفر}]{\ar{أخضر}, \ar{أصفر} — \textquotedblleft{}greens\textquotedblright{} you'd recognize, and a hidden zero}

\label{lesson:AR-C22-akhdar-asfar}



\begin{quote}
Arabic's green word hides an English-style pun. Its yellow word hides something even better — the exact root behind the word \textquotedblleft{}zero\textquotedblright{} itself.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\ar{أخضر}} (\emph{akhḍar}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{green}\textquotedblright{}) comes from the root \textbf{\ar{خ}-\ar{ض}-\ar{ر}} (\emph{kh-ḍ-r}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to be green}\textquotedblright{}). That same root gives \textbf{\ar{خضار}} (\emph{khuḍār}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{vegetables}\textquotedblright{}) — echoing the exact same move English makes when it calls vegetables \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{greens}.\textquotedblright{} The same root also names the mysterious Quranic figure \textbf{\ar{الخِضْر}} (\emph{al-Khiḍr}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the Green One}\textquotedblright{} — traditionally said to be called this because the ground turned green wherever he sat or prayed.
\end{culture}

\begin{culture}
Here's the real surprise: \textbf{\ar{أصفر}} (\emph{aṣfar}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{yellow}\textquotedblright{}) shares its root, \textbf{\ar{ص}-\ar{ف}-\ar{ر}} (\emph{ṣ-f-r}), with \textbf{\ar{صفر}} (\emph{ṣifr}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{zero, empty, void}\textquotedblright{}) — the \textbf{exact} Arabic word that gave English both \textbf{zero} (via Italian \emph{zefiro}/\emph{zero}) and \textbf{cipher} (via Medieval Latin \emph{cifra}). So the same three-letter Arabic root sits behind \textquotedblleft{}yellow\textquotedblright{} and behind the number \textbf{zero} itself. The sources don't fully explain \emph{why} \textquotedblleft{}emptiness\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}yellow\textquotedblright{} share a root — but the shared root itself, connecting Arabic's yellow-word straight back to the origin of \textquotedblleft{}zero,\textquotedblright{} is genuine and well documented.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}akhḍar\textquotedblright{} — green, same root as \textquotedblleft{}khuḍār,\textquotedblright{} vegetables
  \item \textquotedblleft{}aṣfar\textquotedblright{} — yellow, same root as \textquotedblleft{}ṣifr,\textquotedblright{} zero
  \item the connection — \textquotedblleft{}aṣfar, ṣifr, zero, cipher\textquotedblright{} — one Arabic root, reaching all the way into English math vocabulary
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What root does \textbf{\ar{أخضر}} share with \textquotedblleft{}vegetables,\textquotedblright{} and what English phrase does this echo? (\textbf{\ar{خ}-\ar{ض}-\ar{ر}}, \emph{kh-ḍ-r} — echoes English calling vegetables \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{greens}.\textquotedblright{}) What Quranic figure shares this root, and what does his name mean? (\textbf{\ar{الخِضْر}}, \emph{al-Khiḍr} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the Green One}.\textquotedblright{}) What word does \textbf{\ar{أصفر}} share its root with, and what two English words trace back to it? (\textbf{\ar{صفر}}, \emph{ṣifr}, \textquotedblleft{}zero, empty\textquotedblright{} — the source of English \textbf{zero} and \textbf{cipher}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[raʾs · yad · kam ʿumruka?]{The head and the hand}

\label{lesson:AR-R22-the-head-and-the-hand}



\begin{quote}
Touch your head, then your hand, and give the Arabic for each. Both arrived a dozen lessons ago in single words and have not been asked for since.
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=violet!6,colframe=violet!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Across the family: five words older than Arabic}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Arabic} & \textbf{meaning} & \textbf{Hebrew cousin} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{رأس}} \emph{raʾs} & head & \textbf{\he{ראש}} \emph{rosh} \\
\textbf{\ar{يد}} \emph{yad} & hand & \textbf{\he{יד}} \emph{yad} \\
\textbf{\ar{أب}} \emph{ab} & father & \textbf{\he{אב}} \emph{av} \\
\textbf{\ar{أم}} \emph{umm} & mother & \textbf{\he{אם}} \emph{em} \\
\textbf{\ar{أخ}} \emph{akh} & brother & \textbf{\he{אח}} \emph{ach} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

These are not borrowings in either direction. Both languages inherited them, and \textbf{\ar{يد}} is the most striking of the set: spelled and said almost identically on both sides, worn down hardly at all in several thousand years.

\textbf{\ar{رأس}} is the word inside \emph{Rosh Hashanah}, the head of the year.
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,skin=enhanced,colback=violet!6,colframe=violet!45!black,boxrule=0.5pt,arc=1mm,left=6pt,right=6pt,top=4pt,bottom=4pt,fonttitle=\bfseries,title={Across the family: what the roots still build}]
None of these roots is a museum piece.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ar{رئيس}} \emph{raʾīs} — \textbf{president, chief} — is built straight on \emph{head}, the same way English \emph{capital} and \emph{captain} grow out of Latin \emph{caput}.
  \item \textbf{\ar{أم}} and \textbf{\ar{أبو}} still form the \textbf{kunya}, a living honorific: \emph{mother of} and \emph{father of}, plus a child's name.
  \item \textbf{\ar{أخت}} \emph{ukht} is \textbf{\ar{أخ}} with a single letter added — the simplest gendering in the language, against the reshaped templates the colour words needed.
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: an age is a thing you own}]
\textbf{\ar{عمر}} \emph{ʿumr} is \textbf{age, lifetime, life span}, from the root \textbf{\ar{ع}-\ar{م}-\ar{ر}}, tied to living and flourishing.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{كم} \ar{عمرك؟}} \emph{kam ʿumruka?} — literally \textbf{how much is your lifetime?}
\end{quote}

The Romance languages \textbf{have} their years; the Germanic ones \textbf{are} their years. Arabic does neither. It hangs the same \emph{your} suffix on a noun and drops the verb altogether, exactly as the name and wellbeing questions do.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} head, then hand — \emph{raʾs} … \emph{yad}
  \item \emph{Say it:} father, mother, brother, sister — \emph{ab}, \emph{umm}, \emph{akh}, \emph{ukht}
  \item \emph{Say it:} ask a man his age — \emph{kam ʿumruka?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} ask a woman — \emph{kam ʿumruki?}
  \item \emph{Recall:} the word for president, and the body part it is built on
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name which word in this set has changed least from its Hebrew cousin. (\textbf{\ar{يد}} — both \emph{yad}.) Give the word for president and its literal base. (\textbf{\ar{رئيس}}, from \emph{head}.) Say what turns \textbf{\ar{أخ}} into its feminine. (\textbf{One added letter} — \textbf{\ar{أخت}}.) And give the literal wording of the age question. (\textbf{How much is your lifetime}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
